title: The monk who lived on taro
translation: At Shinjō-in there was a senior priest called Jōshin, a very learned man. He loved taro and ate a lot of it. Even when he was lecturing on scripture, he kept a big bowl piled high with it by his knees and read from the text while he ate. When he was ill, he shut himself away for a week or two "for treatment", picked out the best taro he could find, ate even more than usual, and that cured everything. He never gave anyone any. He ate it all himself.

He was very poor. When his teacher was dying, he left him two hundred strings of coins and a house. Jōshin sold the house for a hundred strings, set the whole three hundred aside as taro money, and left it with someone in the city. He had it sent ten strings at a time, ate all the taro he wanted, and spent it on nothing else, until it was all gone. "He's that poor, he comes into three hundred strings, and that's what he does with it," people said. "A real man of faith. You don't see many like him."
Once he took one look at a certain priest and named him Shiroururi. "What's a shiroururi?" someone asked. "No idea," he said. "But if there were such a thing, I'm sure it would look like his face."

He was good-looking, strong and a big eater, wrote a beautiful hand, was a real scholar and spoke better than anyone. He was the leading man of his school, and the temple thought highly of him. But he was an odd one who didn't care what the world thought. He did as he pleased in everything and hardly ever did what anyone told him.

At formal dinners he didn't wait until everyone had been served. As soon as his own tray was set down, he started eating, alone, and when he wanted to leave, he got up, alone, and went. He didn't eat at the monks' set mealtimes either. He ate when he felt like it, in the middle of the night or at dawn. If he was sleepy, he locked himself in, even in the daytime, and whatever was happening, however important, he wouldn't listen to anyone. Once awake, he could go without sleep for nights on end, wandering about humming to himself, his mind clear and calm. None of this was normal, but nobody resented him, and he got away with everything. Perhaps he was simply that good a man.

literal: At Shinjō-in there was a distinguished wise man called the Sōzu Jōshin.
He liked the thing called taro head and ate a lot of it.
Even at lectures on scripture, he piled it high in a big bowl, kept it by his knees, and read the texts while eating.
When he had an illness, he shut himself in for seven or fourteen days, calling it treatment, chose good taro heads as he liked, ate especially many, and cured all his illnesses.
He did not let others eat it; he ate it only by himself.
He was extremely poor, and his teacher, when dying, left him two hundred kan of money and one monk's house; he sold the house for a hundred kan, and

decided on the whole thirty thousand hiki as taro money, deposited it with a person in the capital, had it sent ten kan at a time, and ate taro without running short, and since he did not use it for anything else, the money was all used up.
'Getting three hundred kan when he was poor, and disposing of it like this: truly he is a rare man of the Way', people said.
This Sōzu looked at a certain priest and gave him the name Shiroururi.
When someone asked, 'What is that?', he said, 'I don't know such a thing either. If there were one, it would surely look like this monk's face.'

This Sōzu was good-looking, strong, a big eater, a fine calligrapher, a scholar, and better than others at speaking, and since he was the lamp of the Law of his school, he was highly regarded in the temple too, but he was an eccentric who thought little of the world, (did) everything freely, and almost never followed others.

When he attended service and sat at a banquet, he did not wait until the trays had been set before everyone; once his own was set, he immediately ate alone, and if he wanted to go home, he stood up alone and left.

He did not eat the proper meal and the off-hours meal at fixed times like others; he ate when he wanted to eat, even at midnight or at dawn, and if sleepy, he shut himself in even in the daytime, and whatever important matter there was, he did not listen to what people said.
Once awake, he did not sleep for many nights.
With a clear mind, he walked about humming and so on, a manner not of the ordinary world, but he was not disliked by people and was allowed everything.
Was it that his virtue had reached the utmost?

notes.text: A sub-temple of Ninnaji (sections 52–54). The 1925 edition says it was where retired abbots lived.
Little is known about Jōshin apart from this section. {僧都|そうづ}: one of the highest ranks in the Buddhist clergy, just below {僧正|そうじやう}.
{芋頭|いもがしら}: the big central corm of the taro plant ({里芋|さといも}), with the smaller ones growing around it. The 1925 edition glosses it as 'the parent of the taro'.
'Seven days, two-sevens of days': counting in weeks, as for Buddhist rites. A course of treatment.

A {貫|くわん} was a string of a thousand copper coins with holes in the middle. A {疋|ひき} was ten coins, so 三万疋 is three hundred strings: the two hundred he inherited plus the hundred from the house. A large sum for a poor monk.
{銭|あし}: an old word for money (see section 51).

The 1925 edition: a nonsense nickname that sounds funny and somehow like a monk; there is no point in looking for a meaning. Later commentators have suggested meanings anyway, without agreeing on one.

notes.quote: もしあらましかば、この僧の顔に似てむ
notes.text: ましかば … む: 'if there were…, it would…', a hypothesis against the facts. てむ: 'would surely'. He invents a word and then says what it looks like.
{曲者|くせもの}: here 'an eccentric, a man with his own ways' (the 1925 edition). Modern くせもの also means a suspicious character, or a tricky one.
{斎|とき}: the monks' one proper meal of the day, at midday. {非時|ひじ}: a meal at any other time, such as in the evening (both from the 1925 edition). Jōshin ate when he was hungry.

notes.quote: 徳のいたれりけるにや
notes.text: にや: 'is it that…?', with あらむ left out. The section ends with a guess, not a verdict.
